name: Glamour Bonnet

card.summary: A 1940s vacuum helmet marketed as a way to lower the air pressure around the head, boost circulation and give a rosier complexion.
card.note: A historical curiosity; the maker's circulation claims were never shown in published trials, and a sealed hood connected to a vacuum is an asphyxiation hazard.

quick.overview:
The Glamour Bonnet was a hood-like helmet, sold in the 1940s, that fitted over the head and was connected to a vacuum so that the air pressure around the face and scalp was reduced. Its inventor, reported as Mrs. D. M. Ackerman, said the low pressure would increase blood flow to the skin and so improve the wearer's complexion.

The idea borrowed from the flushed, rosy look associated with high altitude. Nothing in the available historical coverage suggests the device was ever tested in a published study, and it is remembered mainly as one of several mid-century beauty contraptions.
quick.how: Customers sat in a salon or at home with the helmet sealed over the head and the vacuum attached; a small window let them read during the treatment. Sessions were presented as a complexion treatment, to be repeated like other salon routines of the era.
quick.risks: No clinical safety data exist. Coverage of the device points out that a hood connected to a vacuum hose restricts the air available to the wearer, which is the main hazard people raise about it. The device is no longer sold.

lead: The Glamour Bonnet was a 1940s beauty device in the form of a helmet or hood that was placed over the head and connected to a vacuum to lower the surrounding air pressure.[1] Its inventor, credited in popular histories as Mrs. D. M. Ackerman, claimed that the reduced pressure around the head would increase blood flow and thereby improve skin and complexion.[1]

People used it in the hope of a healthier, rosier face: the pitch borrowed the flushed look associated with climbing a mountain or flying at altitude, with circulation to the skin as the proposed mechanism.[1] A small window in the helmet was included so that the customer could read during treatment.[1]
No published clinical study of the device is known, and it survives mostly as an example of the mechanical complexion gadgets sold in the 1930s and 1940s.

chain: Vacuum helmet lowers air pressure around head
Claimed to increase blood flow to facial skin
angle.text: Users wore the helmet in the belief that low pressure would draw more blood to the skin of the face and scalp, producing a fresher colour. The claim came from the manufacturer's marketing and was not backed by published trials.

paras: The Glamour Bonnet was described as a helmet that enclosed the head and was attached to a vacuum hose, reducing the atmospheric pressure around the wearer's head.[1] The stated aim was to imitate the effect on the body of high altitude, thereby increasing blood flow to the skin.[1]
A plastic window allowed the wearer to read while the device was running.[1]

The device is chiefly known today from retrospective roundups of vintage beauty contraptions, which note that the vacuum hose also limited the wearer's air supply.[1] Accounts differ on details such as the inventor's title, and little is documented about sales or how widely it was used.

timeline.event: The Glamour Bonnet vacuum helmet is marketed as a complexion treatment.[1]
